title: Large improvement in ductility of ultra-high strength CoCrNi-base alloy by one-stage grain refinement
abstract: Abstract Pursuing a superior combination of strength and ductility in the ultra-high strength range is always a target, as it brings the benefit of reducing the weight and increasing the safety of the alloy during usage. Composition and process design are important ways to achieve the goal. The CoCrNi-base FCC alloy has low yield strength but very high ductility, so it becomes a high-potential alloy system for this goal. In this work, we use a small addition of Ti to achieve precipitation hardening and a one-stage grain refining process to provide a fine microstructure in the CoCrNi-base alloy. This research reveals that the one-stage grain refining process by rolling and annealing will yield finer initial grains, providing higher strain energy and more nucleation sites for more uniform precipitates and higher recrystallization ratios through cold-rolling and ensuing 600 °C heat treatment. The behavior of annealed texture and grain growth ability is different as well. Under identical conditions, yield strength (YS) and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) are in a comparable range of 1300–1400 and 1800–2000 MPa, while total elongation improves by a factor of 1.5–2 when grain sizes are preliminarily reduced by one-stage grain refinement. The reasons for this improvement are discussed.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) were developed by Yeh et al. in 2004 [ 1 ]. HEAs consist of at least five principal elements, each accounting for from 5 to 35 atomic percentage (at.%). The multi-principal-element design lets HEAs display high entropy effect, severe lattice distortion effect, sluggish diffusion effect, and cocktail effect [ 2 ,  3  ]. With advances in HEAs, medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) with 3 or 4 principal elements have drawn the attention of researchers in recent years since they might provide very high toughness [ 4 ,  5  ]. Other promising characteristics and distinct behaviors are also discovered, such as irradiation resistance, high hardness, and serrated plastic flow at ultra-low temperatures [ 6 ,  7 – 8 ]. In the scope of MEAs, numerous works have been conducted on CoCrNi, derived from the noted CoCrFeMnNi HEA [ 9 ,  10  ]. The CoCrNi MEA possesses superior properties than its quinary, quaternary, and ternary counterparts on account of its even lower stacking fault energy (SFE), which can result in the early domination of twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) and transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) [ 11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 – 15 ]. Consequently, CoCrNi-base MEA is selected in this research because of its popularity, ease of comparison, and exceptional ductility.

To pursue suitable mechanical properties for broader application, grain boundary engineering (GBE) was proposed in 1984 [ 16 ]. It became a strategy to manipulate microstructure to optimize polycrystals, including enhancing ductility [ 17 ], strength [ 18 ], creep resistance [ 19 ], weldability [ 20 ], anti-corrosion behavior [ 21 ], and so on. This concept is also implemented in HEAs and MEAs, numerous works have investigated the control of grain structure and its influence on mechanical behaviors in HEAs and MEAs [ 22 ,  23  ]. The strength of the alloy increases with grain refinement on account of the Hall-Petch effect. The formation of ultra-fine grains through severe plastic deformation [ 24 ,  25 – 26 ] and heterogeneous structure induced by partial recrystallization [ 22 ,  27 ,  28  –] or grain size gradient [ 30 ,  31 – 32 ] are popular methods to break through the strength-ductility dilemma via GBE in HEAs and MEAs.

Precipitation strengthening is another fundamental mechanism to improve the mechanical properties of the alloys, which results from the interaction between dislocations and precipitates. The precipitates hinder the dislocation movement and thus increase strength by shearing or bypassing mechanism, depending on the coherency and size [ 33 ]. Although not addressed in this study, it is worth mentioning that the effect of GBE stated in the previous section and the impact of precipitation can be designed to coexist by controlling grain boundary wetting [ 34 ,  35 – 36 ]. Generally, in most studies, the control of intermetallics, including size, morphology, distribution, and fraction are focused on, which have profound influences on mechanical behavior [ 37 ,  38 ,  39 ,  40 ,  41 ,  42 – 43 ]. Consequently, the temporal evolution of the precipitates is a worthwhile topic to be discussed [ 44 ]. In this study, η-Ni 3 Ti precipitation is selected, as a small addition of Ti could generate a high volume fraction of precipitates and its various morphologies under different heat-treatment conditions, including small particle, needle-like (cellular), Widmanstätten, and large platelets could be monitored [ 45 ,  46 ,  47 – 48 ].

Based on the above, we use a small addition of Ti to achieve precipitation hardening and a one-stage grain refining process to inhibit the void nucleation at the potential sites by reducing the initial grain size in the CoCrNi-base alloy. This is expected to achieve a high combination of strength and ductility in the ultra-high strength range. The real mechanisms are investigated and discussed.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: The composition of the MEA was Co 32.2 Cr 30.6 Ni 35.2 Ti 2.0  (at.%), adjusted from our previous alloy, which displayed an FCC and η-Ni 3 Ti dual-phase structure [ 49 ]. The design of the composition was based on CoCrNi MEA, and Ti was intended to form η-Ni 3 Ti precipitates to strengthen the alloy. In the present alloy, Ni content was increased, whereas Co and Cr contents were decreased so as to suppress the formation of the  σ  phase. By calculation, this alloy had a VEC (Valence Electron Concentration) of 8.334, indicating that the  σ  phase would not be generated [ 50 ].

The alloy was fabricated from pure elements (>99.9 weight percentage) via vacuum arc melting under an argon atmosphere. After solidification in a water-cooled copper mold, the specimen was homogenized at 1200 °C for 6 h, followed by water quenching. To understand the effect of initial grain size on the alloy’s final properties, cold-rolling with a 60% thickness reduction was performed, followed by 10-min annealing at 1100 °C and water quenching to reduce grain size. This process was called “one-stage grain refinement,” and the sample that went through this process was named as FG (fine grain). On the contrary, the specimen that did not undergo the grain-refining procedure and had a larger grain size was named as CG (coarse grain). Cold-rolling with a 70% thickness reduction was then applied to both CG and FG samples. Afterward, the samples of CG and FG were aged for 6, 12, and 72 h at 600 °C and investigated to compare their microstructures and properties. The flowchart of experimental procedures and the reasons for choosing 6, 12, and 72 h conditions are presented in the supplementary materials Fig.  S1  and  S2 .

Various examinations were conducted to identify the microstructures and mechanical properties. Electron backscatter diffraction (ZEISS GeminiSEM 300 equipped with Oxford Instrument Symmetry S2 EBSD detector) was used to analyze the initial grain size, cold-rolled structure, recrystallization, and texture of the FCC matrix. The samples were ground using silicon carbide grit sandpapers up to #4000, and then polished with suspensions of 0.3 and 0.05 μm alumina. Vibratory final-polishing with 0.02 μm silica was conducted at the end. Scanning electron microscope (ZEISS GeminiSEM 300 and JEOL JSM IT100) and transmission electron microscope (JEOL JEM-F200) were utilized to observe the precipitation, fracture surfaces, and deformation mode. For SEM observation of precipitation, the samples were electrically etched in a 20% H 3 PO 4  ethanol solution after being polished with alumina. The TEM samples were mechanically ground to a thickness of 60 μm and then thinned by the twin-jet method using a mixture of HClO 4  and C 2 H 6 O (1:9) at 20 V and − 25 ℃.

Mitutoyo HV 100 Vickers hardness tester was used to measure the hardness with a 5-kg load and a holding time of 12 s. Tensile tests were performed on a Shimadzu AGS-100kNX machine at a strain rate of 10 −3  s −1  at 25 °C with a 10 mm extensometer. In addition, a digital image correlation (DIC) system was utilized to obtain strain distributions on the specimen during tensile tests using an AOS PROMON U1000 high-speed camera and the analysis software of GOM correlation. The testing specimens were dog-bone-shaped with a 19 mm gauge length. The tests were repeated two to three times to ensure accuracy and reproducibility.

sections.heading: Two microstructures with coarse and fine grains
paragraphs: Figure  1 a and b present the inverse pole figure (IPF) maps of CG and FG samples, indicating that the initial grain sizes in the two conditions are > 500 μm without one-stage grain refinement process and 16 ± 10.7 μm after receiving one-stage grain refinement process. The difference illustrates that the one-stage grain refinement (60% cold-rolling and 1100 °C-10-min annealing) reduces the grain size by more than 30 times. With the dissimilarity in grain size, CG and FG samples undergo an identical 70% cold-rolling and then are investigated by EBSD with 0.2 μm step size, including IPF maps and kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps as shown in Fig.  1 c–f. The cold-rolled structures are evident in the figures, such as elongated grains along the rolling direction, distorted or fragmented grain boundaries, and in-grain deformation shear bands. These regions are usually highly strained and have higher dislocation densities, so they appear as black unidentified points in EBSD due to poorly indexed crystallographic orientations and have higher strain energy around them. Compared to CG, a single deformed structure is finer but denser in FG, which is developed from its smaller grain size prior to 70% cold-rolling. This results in a more fragmented and more energetically homogeneous deformed structure. The KAM analysis is in good agreement with this concept. The KAM values of Fig.  1 d and f are 1.8° ± 0.81° and 2.1° ± 1.36°, respectively. In Fig.  1 d, the white arrows point at regions with lower strain energy inside CG reported by KAM maps. It reveals that the total strain energy of FG is higher, and the low-strain domains in FG are fewer in number and smaller in size. Figure 1 The IPF maps for  a  CG  b  FG initial grains and  c  CG  e  FG after 70% cold-rolling, and the KAM maps of  d  CG  f  FG after 70% cold-rolling.

sections.heading: Evolution of the FCC matrix
paragraphs: Figure  2  and  3  are the results of EBSD analysis after aging. In supplementary materials, Table.  S1  presents the grain boundary analysis from EBSD. The step size is 0.2 μm, and the quantified results in Fig.  3  and Table.  S1  are from the raw data combined from five measurements at different areas of the sample. The combined data are analyzed as a whole, so only the average grain diameter has standard deviations. Figure  2 a and d are the IPF maps of CG and FG after 600 °C 6 h aging. The graphs demonstrate that a lot of cold-rolling induced features are still retained. This can be attributed to the formation of precipitates, which adversely affects dislocation movement, resulting in slower annealing behavior [ 51 ,  52 – 53 ]. Besides, the multi-element design also slows down the process due to sluggish diffusion and lattice distortion [ 52 ,  53  ]. Fig.  2 g and j are the grain orientation spread (GOS) maps that mark the recrystallized grains with colors after 6 h of aging, using 2° as a criterion [ 54 ,  55  ]. GOS maps show that recrystallization tends to occur within black regions, which correspond to distorted grain boundaries, shear bands, and high-dislocation-density regions imposed during cold-rolling. These areas have high energy stored, becoming preferential nucleation sites during recrystallization [ 56 ,  57  ]. Since there are more available nucleation sites in FG, a higher recrystallization ratio is achieved. The ratio of recrystallized regions is shown in Fig.  3 a for CG6h and FG6h, with 6.2% and 16.9%, respectively. The fractions of low-angle grain boundary (LAGB, θ = 2°~15°), high-angle grain boundary (HAGB, θ > 15°, but excludes Σ3), and CSL Σ3 special boundary (twin boundary, 60° <1 1 1>) are presented in Table.  S1 . LAGB is related to the deformed state, such as dislocation substructure, and will gradually diminish and transform into HAGB with heat treatment. Some of the HAGB will turn into Σ3, which is one of the special categories of HAGB and has a lower boundary energy. Thus, Σ3 fraction will increase with the extent of annealing. The fraction shown in Table.  S1  corresponds to the recrystallized fraction shown in Fig.  3 a. CG6h retains more LAGB of 17.5% higher, while FG6h holds more HAGB and Σ3 of 14.5% and 3% higher, respectively. Figure 2 The IPF maps of  a–c  CG,  d–f  FG, and the GOS of  g–i  CG,  j–l  FG after aging at 600 ℃ for 6, 12, and 72 h. Figure 3 The plots showing the quantified results from EBSD analysis.

Figure  2 b and e are the IPF maps of CG and FG after 600 °C 12 h aging, while Fig.  2 h and k are the GOS maps that reveal the fully recrystallized grains with colors by 2° criteria. These graphs show that non-recrystallized regions are still dominant in CG12h, while recrystallized grains begin to take over in FG12h. The recrystallization ratios are 10.8% and 37.4% for CG12h and FG12h, respectively, as plotted in Fig.  3 a. In CG6h and FG6h, the recrystallized grains are mainly submicron in size and are located in the black regions (characterized by deformed structures, such as shear bands, distorted grain boundaries, dislocations, and so on), which have the highest strain energy and become preferential nucleation sites. In CG12h and FG12h, both start to form newly recrystallized grains of micro-scale size outside the black regions, such as in the middle of two closely spaced black lines. Moreover, due to the higher strain energy of non-black regions in FG before aging, as indicated in Fig.  1 c–f, it is easier for FG to recrystallize in these areas. In contrast, more heat treatment is required for CG. Consequently, in addition to more preferential sites, recrystallization outside the black areas also contributes to the higher recrystallization ratio in FG12h. The boundary analysis in Table.  S1  shows the trends: firstly, both CG12h and FG12h show decreases in LAGB and increases in HAGB and Σ3 compared to their 6h counterparts. Secondly, in FG12h, LAGB is 27.5% lower compared to CG12h, whereas HAGB and Σ3 are 17.5% and 10% higher, respectively. This corresponds to the more recrystallized grains in FG12h, and indicates that the discrepancies in boundaries expand with increased difference in recrystallization ratio between CG and FG.

Fig.  2 c and f are the IPF maps of CG and FG after prolonged 600 °C 72 h aging, while Fig.  2 i and l are the GOS maps that reveal the fully recrystallized grains using a 2° standard. Although pieces of the deformed structure are still preserved inside CG72h, both CG72h and FG72h have exceeded 75% recrystallization, with the ratio difference shrinking to 7.4%. In addition, the differences in LAGB, HAGB, and Σ3 are also reduced to 9.5%, 7.2%, and 2.3%, respectively. This indicates that the degree of annealing is initially strongly influenced by the strain energy prior to heat treatment, leading to considerable differences between CG and FG at short times (6 and 12 h). The initial fine-grain (FG) possesses higher and more uniform strain energy in the deformed structure due to one-stage grain refinement, resulting in faster annealing, whereas the discrepancy can be reduced over time. However, as shown in Fig.  3 b–c, the grain growth exhibits the opposite behavior; CG has a larger grain size, and the difference expands throughout aging in terms of average grain diameter and maximum grain diameter. This behavior also stems from differences in the cold-rolled structure. Fewer preferential nucleation sites inside the CG lead to a reduction in mutual grain-to-grain restrictions on grain growth. The idea will be discussed in more detail in Section " Grain size and texture ".

sections.heading: Texture of the FCC matrix
paragraphs: To examine the difference between CG and FG after heat treatment, the textures of the recrystallized FCC grains are also compared. ODF (Orientation Distribution Function) maps of the crystallographic orientations measured by EBSD are shown in Fig.  4 . Each scan covers an area of 100*300 μm 2 , and five scans are performed on the CG72h, FG-rolled, and FG72h; twenty scans are performed on the CG-rolled due to its >500 μm initial grain. The raw data are averaged before being generated into ODF maps. Since the objective is to compare recrystallization behavior, only the texture data of recrystallized grains (GOS<2°) is selected from CG72h and FG72h. In the rolled state, the deformation texture is influenced by the SFE (Stacking Fault Energy). In the low SFE alloy, plastic deformation occurs by shear banding and twinning. According to these deformation mechanisms, texture components on the  α -fiber (<110> // ND) are usually observed, which are related to the plane slip [ 58 ,  59  ]. In ODF maps,  α -fiber locates at ( φ 1 =0°~90°,  Φ =45°,  φ 2 =0°), and ( φ 1 =0°~90°,  Φ =90°,  φ 2 =45°). Another common fiber is the  γ -fiber (<111> // ND), which is strongly correlated with the shear stress and the formation of deformation twins [ 57 ]. It is reported that twin lamellas will rotate toward the rolling plane and that twins occur on the close-packed slip planes in FCC alloys; therefore, twins develop the <111> // ND fiber. In ODF maps, the  γ -fiber is located at ( φ 1 =0°~90°,  Φ =60°,  φ 2 =45°). The ODFs of CG-rolled and FG-rolled in Fig.  4  are consistent with the literature; both demonstrate the dominance of  α -fiber and  γ -fiber. Additionally, after aging for 72 h, although the intensity decreases, CG72h and FG72h still retain these deformed texture characteristics within the recrystallized grains. However, CG72h shows lower intensity and a more random distribution compared to FG72h. The retention of deformation-rolled textures is usually associated with nucleation and grain growth, which will be further described in Section " Grain size and texture ". Figure 4 The ODF of the FCC matrix from the EBSD measurements.

sections.heading: Evolution of η-precipitate
paragraphs: In CG12h, the total η fraction drastically increases to 16.3%, with 7.7% and 3.7% growth for the η-particle and η-needle, respectively. The increase in η-particle is greater than that of η-needle owing to the difference in the required energy mentioned above. Although there are still some PFZs remaining, the microstructure of the η-Ni 3 Ti phase in CG is becoming more similar to that of FG at 12h. In FG12h, the total η fraction slightly increases to 20.8%. Both morphologies only have a minute growth of 1.6% and 0.5% for η-particle and η-needle, respectively. This indicates that FG12h has gradually reached the saturation of the η-Ni 3 Ti phase. As plotted in Fig.  5 g–h, both the discrepancies in total η fraction and average diameter are reduced between CG12h and FG12h. In Table.  S2 , nearly all the differences between CG12h and FG12h shrink; the only enlarged distinction is the average length of the η-needle. This is associated with the growth of already existing η-needles in FG12h, whereas CG12h prefers to precipitate new tiny η-needles at this stage.

After prolonged aging to 72 h, the total η-phase fraction is 22.6% and 24.0% for CG72h and FG72h, respectively. Most of the increment results from the increase in η-needle, both reaching ~11.5%. The η-particle increases by only 0.7% in CG72h; moreover, a decrease of 1.9% is measured in FG72h. The findings can be ascribed to the coalescence of η-particles during their growth, transforming the particles into needles, which is called the “linear arrangement” growth mechanism [ 61 ]. At 72 h, some η-needles have grown over 2 μm in length for CG72h and FG72h, while newly formed η-needles are still in the hundreds of nanometers. Thereby, the average lengths of the η-needle remain 513.8 nm and 602.9 nm for CG72h and FG72h, respectively, with the standard deviations exceeding 400 nm for both. According to the parameters in Fig.  5 g–h and Table.  S2 , the microstructure of the η-Ni 3 Ti in CG and FG becomes similar after 72 h of aging, with respect to morphology, fraction, and size. The results indicate that the trend in precipitation behavior is similar to that of recrystallization. The higher and more uniform strain energy induced by cold-rolling from the initial fine grain (FG) accelerates the precipitation process and also inhibits PFZ formation in short-time aging by uniformly distributing strain energy, which will positively affect the mechanical properties of FG. However, the difference will be reduced over time.

sections.heading: Crystal structure of η-precipitate
Mechanical properties
paragraphs: The tensile properties of CG and FG are presented in Fig.  7 (a) and Table  1 . The 6 h and 12 h aging conditions are chosen because of their high hardness, as shown in Fig.  S2 , suggesting potential application in the ultra-high-strength range. The results of mechanical properties are strongly linked to microstructures, which are influenced by the differences in initial grain size between CG and FG, created by the one-stage grain refinement process. Overall, the uniform elongation, yield strength (YS), and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) are comparable for CG and FG. Nonetheless, there is a significant discrepancy in terms of total elongation. The limited uniform elongation of ~ 4% in all samples results from the insufficient recrystallization. The lack of recrystallization will lead to localized high stresses and nonuniform strain distribution within the alloy [ 66 ], thereby reducing the uniform elongation and promoting crack initiation. Moreover, although a special orientation relationship exists between the FCC matrix and the η-precipitate, the non-coherent phase boundary and the brittle nature of the η-phase facilitate crack formation at the interfaces [ 46 ,  47 – 48 ], which also results in limited uniform elongation. The DIC images in Fig.  7 a demonstrate the onset of strain localization at UTS for both CG12h and FG12h, indicating the end of uniform deformation. Figure 7 The  a  tensile tests and DIC analysis, and  b  quantitative strengthening calculations. Table 1 YS, UTS, uniform elongation, and total elongation of the tensile tests YS (MPa) UTS (MPa) Uniform elongation (%) Total elongation (%) CG6h 1353 1879 4.4 6.2 CG12h 1367 1908 4.5 5.5 FG6h 1428 2016 4.3 8.9 FG12h 1303 1836 4.4 12.0

Figure  7 a reveals that FG possesses an improved total elongation: CG has only 5 ~ 6%, whereas FG increases to 9 ~ 12%. The superior properties in FG6h and FG12h are attributed to a comparatively higher recrystallization ratio and inhibition of precipitation free zones (PFZs). Although the recrystallized fractions in FG6h and FG12h are not yet fully dominant, the recrystallized grains still provide more plasticity to reduce the pile-up stress for crack initiation and dissipate stress during crack propagation [ 66 ]. On the other hand, the PFZs are softer than in other regions, which will result in localized deformation and hence enhancement in crack activity, including nucleation and propagation [ 21 ,  24 ,  26   ]. Additionally, it is reported that η-precipitate inhibits crack propagation during deformation to some extent [ 65 ]; the presence of PFZs suppresses this beneficial effect on ductility. Therefore, inhibition of PFZs improves mechanical performance in FG. In Fig.  7 a, the DIC images show that strain in CG12h is highly concentrated at the fracture point, while more parts of FG12h undergo a high degree of deformation and exhibit necking behavior. The findings correlate with differences in crack activity: rapid crack activity is observed in CG, driven by PFZs and the low recrystallization ratio. The quick crack activity leads to early fracture with low total elongation. On the contrary, the activity of cracks slows down in FG6h and FG12h, giving rise to a better total elongation in FG.

sections.heading: Grain size and texture
paragraphs: From the EBSD analysis in Fig.  2  and Fig.  3 , it is interesting to note that there are two kinds of grain size in the over 75% recrystallized CG72h and FG72h. The grain diameter can be classified into submicron and micron scales. The smaller submicron grains are located in the high-strain black regions (characterized by deformed structures such as shear bands, distorted grain boundaries, dislocations, and so on), which have more potential nucleation sites, leading to numerous and rapid recrystallization. The formation of abundant recrystallized grains results in restricted grain growth. In contrast, other regions have fewer nucleation sites, thereby reducing mutual grain-to-grain restraint on grain growth, and grains of several micrometers to tens of micrometers are observed in these areas. The lack of black regions in CG, due to the > 500 μm grain size before cold rolling, results in a larger fraction of micro-scale grains and fewer submicron grains after heat treatment. This characteristic explains the larger grain size of CG after aging, shown in Fig.  3 b–c. Another interesting point is that even after 72 h of heat treatment, the average grain diameters of both CG72h and FG72h are still 2.7 ± 2.42 and 2.2 ± 1.61 μm, respectively. The grain size is significantly smaller than in other studies with similar alloy systems. This can be associated with the dragging force exerted on grain boundaries, coming from the precipitates, known as the Zener pinning [ 51 ,  52 – 53 ]. In addition, the pinning pressure is proportional to the precipitate phase fraction [ 61 ,  70  ]. Consequently, the smaller grain size can be ascribed to the high fraction, > 20%, of the η-precipitate.

The resistance to grain growth in this alloy contributes to the preservation of the cold-rolled texture shown in Fig.  4 . It is reported that retained deformation texture is associated with a lack of preferential grain growth, which relies on rapid migration of grain boundaries [ 71 ,  72  ]. As discussed earlier, due to retardation by the η-precipitate and sluggish diffusion in the multi-element alloy, the preferential grain growth to form other dominant textures is inhibited in this study. Consequently, the recrystallized grains in both CG72h and FG72h still possess deformed textures. Furthermore, more retained deformed textures are observed in the recrystallized grains in FG72h than in those of CG72h, for several reasons. As discussed above, grain growth is more difficult in FG, thereby imposing greater restrictions on preferential growth. In addition, more uniform cold-rolled structures of FG are observed in Fig.  1 . Studies have pointed out that a more energetically homogeneous deformation structure will suppress preferential growth [ 71 ,  73  ]. It is also reported that nuclei tend to have orientations similar to those of the deformed matrix at grain boundaries [ 72 ,  74 ,  75   ]. Because the grain size before cold rolling is smaller in FG and larger in CG, more nucleation will occur at grain boundaries in FG subsequently, preserving more deformed texture components.

sections.heading: Fracture surfaces
paragraphs: Figure  8  presents the fracture surfaces of the tensile tests, showing that all conditions exhibit some small dimples, which are considered as the features of ductile fracture [ 27 ,  76  ]. In similar alloy systems, it is observed that even when the ductility of the alloy is limited, the small dimples still form [ 49 ,  77 ,  78   ], as is the case for CG in this study. This observation can be explained by the high toughness and ductility of the FCC matrix in CoCrNi-base alloys. In Section " Mechanical properties ", the difference in crack activity between CG and FG is discussed. The PFZs, low recrystallization ratio, and the higher contribution of dislocations to strength give rise to rapid crack initiation and propagation and limited total elongation in CG. Figure  8  shows that, besides small dimples, a large fraction of cleavage-like morphology is present in CG as indicated by white arrows, whereas FG only reveals a limited scale. The formation of cleavage-like regions comes from highly localized plastic deformation and rapid crack propagation; consequently, the presence of cleavage-like areas explains the higher crack activity and reduced mechanical properties of CG. Figure 8 Fracture surfaces of the tensile specimens:  a  CG6h,  b  CG12h,  c  FG6h, and  d  FG12h.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this study, one-stage grain refining was used to produce a small initial grain size. The grain size of FG (Fine Grain) before cold-rolling and aging treatment is smaller by more than 30 times than that of CG (Coarse Grain). Room temperature tensile tests show that the samples underwent one-stage grain refining not only achieve high strength, but also improve their total elongation. Key findings and reasons are listed: The reduced initial grains result in a higher strain energy, a more fragmented and more energetically homogeneous cold-rolling structure in FG. This promotes recrystallization during short-time aging at 600 °C. However, disparity diminishes after prolonged aging. FG facilitates earlier, denser, and more homogeneous precipitation of η-Ni 3 Ti during short-time aging. Additionally, FG effectively suppresses precipitation-free zones (PFZs). Nevertheless, with extended aging, the differences in precipitate morphology, size, and fraction between CG and FG gradually shrink. Both CG and FG retain deformed texture (α-fiber and γ-fiber) after extensive recrystallization due to restricted grain growth. The stronger texture retention in FG is attributed to higher grain growth resistance and more nucleation at grain boundaries. Both CG and FG display comparable uniform elongation (~ 4.4%) and ultra-high strength range of yield strength (1300–1400 MPa) and ultimate tensile strength (1800–2000 MPa). However, FG achieves 1.5–2 times higher total elongation. This improvement arises from a higher recrystallized fraction, the suppression of PFZs, and reduced contribution from dislocation strengthening. All these inhibit rapid crack initiation and propagation. CG exhibits pronounced cleavage-like features associated with rapid crack initiation and propagation. In contrast, FG shows suppressed cleavage-like fracture and prevailed uniformly distributed plastic deformation, consistent with slower crack activity and enhanced fracture resistance. Therefore, FG displays better total elongation.

tables.caption: YS, UTS, uniform elongation, and total elongation of the tensile tests
